Think of a building. Before the walls go up, before the roof is placed, before anything else is built, workers lay a foundation — a solid base on which everything else rests. If the foundation is weak or missing, the whole building collapses. If it is strong, everything built on top of it is secure.

"Basis" is that foundation — but for non-physical things. It is the underlying idea, reason, principle, or fact on which everything else rests: a decision, a belief, an argument, a relationship, a system, or an action.

When you identify the basis of something, you are identifying its root — the thing it cannot exist without.

"Basis" has a few closely related meanings. They all share the same core idea of a foundation, but they appear in different settings.

1. The Reason or Grounds for Something

The basis of a decision, claim or belief is the fact or reason it rests on.

  • "On what basis did they reject your application?" (= for what reason?)
  • "There is no scientific basis for that claim." (= nothing supports it)
  • "She was promoted on the basis of her results." (= because of her results)

2. The Starting Point Something Is Built From

The basis of a plan, story or system is the main part or idea it grows out of.

  • "The novel formed the basis of the film."
  • "Trust is the basis of any friendship."

3. The Way or Pattern in Which Something Is Done

In phrases like on a daily basis or on a voluntary basis, basis describes how or how often something happens.

  • "The machines are checked on a weekly basis." (= every week)
  • "She works on a part-time basis."
  • "Places are given on a first-come, first-served basis."

4. In Mathematics

In linear algebra, a basis is a set of vectors from which every other vector in a space can be built. This is a technical use you will meet only in maths and physics.
The plural is bases (pronounced BAY-seez) — the same spelling as the plural of base, but said differently.
Basis = the foundation — the reason, starting point or pattern — on which something rests.
